name: Helix Corp Compliance Tier Pressed Day Set
description:
The quintessential Tier 3 corporate uniform, issued with minor variations across a dozen corponation subsidiaries. A collarless button-front shirt in Helix Corp's proprietary 'administratum weave' — a mid-weight polysynth blend in muted slate-blue that resists wrinkling and absorbs approximately forty percent of ambient sweat. The shirt's collar sits slightly too high and the cuffs slightly too narrow, a cut optimized for a body-scanning algorithm rather than a human tailor. Straight-leg trousers in matching slate-grey with a permanent crease ironed in at the factory, worn smooth at the inner thigh from daily transit seating. A single-button blazer in the same grey-blue family, mass-produced in four standardized fits, with a subtle Helix Corp embossed chevron on the left breast pocket. Footwear is the Cordis Autofit Dress Oxford in matte charcoal, the laces replaced with magnetic closures after the originals frayed. A lanyard with a printed-polymer ID badge completes the look — the badge worn front-facing at chest height as policy dictates.

Up close, the seams show stress at the shoulders and the blazer lining has begun to pill. The neural port collar-notch at the back of the neck has been hand-cut and messily finished with iron-on binding tape rather than factory-finished, a common modification for BCI-equipped workers that Helix Corp refuses to accommodate in their standard issue. The shoes show buffing marks where scuffs have been polished out repeatedly. This is a person who has worn this outfit, or one exactly like it, every working day for years.
functionality: Wrinkle-resistant and sweat-absorbent fabric for long transit and desk shifts. Magnetic closures for quick security checkpoint compliance. BCI port notch (hand-modified). Badge lanyard anchor loop built into collar stay. Scuff-resistant shoe cap.
what_it_says: This is someone who follows the rules because breaking them costs more than it's worth. The outfit signals full compliance with corponation dress code, mid-tier aspirationlessness, and the quiet exhaustion of someone who has stopped expecting the uniform to fit. The hand-cut BCI notch is the only visible act of personal agency.
worn_by: any Tier 3 office drone required to present as professional
price_range: Φ 180–Φ 260 (often partially subsidized by employer as 'uniform allowance')
story_hooks: A character wearing this outfit is pulled aside by a Helix Corp HR compliance bot that flags their hand-cut BCI notch as an 'unauthorized uniform modification' — the fine is small but the precedent is terrifying.

Two people in nearly identical versions of this outfit meet in a transit corridor and realize they work for competing subsidiaries of the same corponation — the badge chevrons are almost identical, the cut marginally different.
Someone is given a slightly better version of this outfit — same color, slightly better fabric — as a quiet signal that they are being considered for a Tier 4 evaluation. No one tells them directly.

physical_description.visual_profile: A standardized corporate silhouette: clean lines, muted authority, algorithmic precision. The wearer appears pressed into uniformity—neat but slightly undersized, as if tailored by committee rather than craft. Conveys compliance and administrative function without warmth or individuality.
physical_description.fit: Precisely tailored to a body-scanning algorithm: collarless shirt sits high at the neck, cuffs narrow at the wrist. Blazer cut in four standard sizes, likely not a perfect match. Trousers sit straight-legged with a permanent factory crease worn smooth from repetitive seating. Compression-adjacent without being performance wear.
physical_description.primary_material: Administratum weave polysynth blend (proprietary Helix Corp formulation) for shirt and blazer; matching slate-grey synthetic for trousers. Matte charcoal synthetic leather for Cordis Autofit dress oxfords.
physical_description.texture: Shirt fabric is smooth, slightly stiff from anti-wrinkle treatment, engineered to resist pilling and moisture. Seams show stress fractures at shoulders. Blazer lining pilled from years of friction. Shoes buffed to a low sheen with visible polishing marks masking scuff wear.
physical_description.color_scheme: Muted slate-blue and slate-grey throughout—a corporate palette designed for visual blandness and easy laundry identification across subsidiary offices. No accent colors, no patterns. Intentional chromatic monotony.
physical_description.closures: Single-button blazer closure. Button-front shirt (standard polymer buttons, slightly yellowed). Magnetic closure on dress oxfords (factory replacement for frayed original laces).
distinctive_features: Embossed Helix Corp chevron on left breast pocket—subtle, institutional branding
Hand-cut neural port collar-notch at back of neck with crude iron-on binding tape (unauthorized worker modification)
Lanyard with printed-polymer ID badge worn front-facing at chest—mandatory policy compliance
Permanent factory crease in trousers worn smooth at inner thigh from daily transit seating
Stress fractures visible at shoulder seams
Buffing marks on shoe leather from repeated scuff removal
Pilled blazer lining visible at edges
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3 working-class corporate. Standard issue, mass-produced, algorithmically fitted rather than tailored. Affordable uniformity. Not aspirational, not salvage.
physical_description.cultural_context: Helix Corp administrative worker, likely BCI-augmented (evidenced by neural port modification). Signals compliance, predictability, mid-tier corporate function. Wearer has internalized the uniform—years of identical days in identical outfits. No room for self-expression within dress code parameters.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and worn. Not damaged, but lived-in. Seams stressed, lining pilled, shoes scuffed and re-polished. The uniform of someone who has worn it every working day for years without complaint or customization beyond the practical neural port cut.
